lesson.title: Connecting allergy information with hygiene
lesson.reading: あれるぎーじょうほうとえいせいをつなぐ

objectives.text: Explain allergy risks and the need to share information
Check foods whose ingredients are not visible
Explain handwashing and separation of raw foods

sections.title: Do not judge safety from a small quantity
sections.body: A food allergy causes symptoms in response to a trigger food. Severe reactions may affect breathing and can be life-threatening. Do not treat an allergy like a preference: confirm whether an allergy exists and which foods are involved at booking or arrival. If only the staff member who heard it remembers, another server may make an error. Match the person, ingredient and dish accurately, and share that information with the kitchen and service staff. Do not personally promise that a small amount is safe. Treat the anaphylactic shock mentioned in the source as a serious, life-threatening condition. Do not leave breathing abnormalities or similar signs unattended on the assumption that a small amount is harmless; follow the facility’s emergency procedure and instructions from 119 or other emergency responders.

sections.title: Ingredients not apparent from appearance
sections.body: Egg, milk, wheat, peanuts and seafood are among ingredients whose presence may not be clear from a dish name. Wheat may be in bread and noodles, but also coatings, wrappers, breadcrumbs and some condiments. Do not assume every soy sauce or miso has the same ingredients: check the actual products and recipe. The manual’s ingredient examples prompt checks; they are not the latest legal list of mandatory labels. Verify current official rules separately before stating statutory counts or revision dates to guests. The Type 1 source also gives soybeans and nuts as examples. The 2024 Type 2 edition lists eight items: egg, milk, wheat, buckwheat, peanuts, shrimp, crab and walnuts. Learn this with the source edition identified. A change on April 1, 2026 added cashew nuts to the specified ingredients for processed-food labeling. There are transitional measures for switching labels, so absence of a name on an older product’s label does not guarantee absence of that ingredient. Distinguish the statutory scope of processed-food labeling from the restaurant’s task of checking the individual guest’s allergies. Do not skip checks for a reported food merely because it is outside the listed items. For wheat, look beyond bread and noodles to dumpling and spring-roll wrappers, okonomiyaki, tempura, sauces and dressings, checking actual products and recipes.

sections.title: Hands and food handling
sections.body: Wash hands before and after food handling and after using the toilet. Understand the purpose and procedure for washing and hand disinfection, and follow the facility’s method. Do not assume alcohol makes handwashing unnecessary. Store each food at suitable temperatures and conditions, and separate raw meat and fish from other foods. Do not invent temperatures or times from a source that gives no numerical conditions. Check the hygiene procedure and ask the responsible person before working with unfamiliar storage requirements.

sections.title: Keep the check before serving
sections.body: Even if the dish was checked for suitability, delivery to the wrong table defeats information-sharing. Match the guest and dish at ordering, preparation and service. If a point remains unclear, do not guess because service is busy; check with the responsible staff. Hygiene is not limited to opening time. Washing at task changes, separating foods and maintaining cleanliness support both a comfortable meal and food-poisoning prevention.

terms.reading: しょくもつあれるぎー
terms.meaning: Symptoms caused by a reaction to a particular food
Materials used to make a food or dish
Ensuring responsible people have the same necessary information

example.situation: A guest who reported a wheat allergy orders a dish with sauce. The menu name does not mention wheat.
steps: Confirm and record the trigger ingredient and the guest concerned.
Ask the kitchen to check products and recipes, including sauce and coatings.
Share the results and match the dish to the intended guest before service.

practice.prompt: Explain what is unverified when someone says, “There is no wheat in the dish name, so it is safe.” Then name three task changes requiring handwashing.
expectedPoints: Check condiments, coatings and wrappers too
Do not guarantee safety alone; share with the kitchen

questions.prompt: The dish name does not mention wheat. What should you do?
choices: Guarantee it is wheat-free
Check actual ingredients and the recipe
Do not check condiments
Guarantee safety after removing the coating
questions.explanation: A name does not reveal condiments. Neither appearance nor removing one part establishes safety.

questions.prompt: What is needed after receiving an allergy report?
choices: Have only the listener remember it
Check appearance alone
Share the trigger, person and dish with kitchen and service staff
Wait until the next visit before passing it on
questions.explanation: Connect the person and dish so information is not lost between preparation and service.

choices: Alcohol alone replaces washing even after toilet use
One wash at opening lasts until closing
Decide only by a daily count, not task changes
Wash before/after food handling and after toilet use using the facility’s procedure
questions.explanation: Wash according to tasks and exposure opportunities. A count alone or disinfection alone is insufficient.

questions.prompt: How should raw meat and fish be stored?
choices: Under appropriate food-specific conditions, separate from other foods
In one container without checking temperature
Anywhere space is available
Ignore temperature if the manual supplies no number
questions.explanation: Use suitable conditions and separation. Ask the responsible person or consult procedures for unknown temperatures.

questions.prompt: A guest reports an allergy to buckwheat or walnuts. What should you do?
choices: Confirm the guest’s trigger foods and ask the kitchen about actual ingredients and service conditions
Ignore foods absent from the material’s short examples
Check only wheat
Personally guarantee safety if the amount is small
questions.explanation: The examples are starting points for checking. Use the guest’s report to guide necessary checks and sharing.

questions.prompt: How should the 2024 eight-item list and current labeling rules be handled?
choices: The 2024 list must remain fixed forever
Distinguish source editions and regulatory changes, and check products and the guest’s conditions
An absent label name always proves absence, even during transition
Base all restaurant checks solely on the number of processed-food labeling items
questions.explanation: Check amendments including the 2026 cashew addition and transitional measures. Do not confuse labeling scope with guest checks.

questions.prompt: Which statement about severe food-allergy reactions is appropriate?
choices: They are preferences, so the guest should endure them
Staff can always guarantee a small amount is safe
Breathing abnormalities can be life-threatening; do not leave them unattended based on your own judgment, and activate emergency procedures
Knowing the term anaphylactic shock makes an emergency call unnecessary
questions.explanation: Understand the possible danger to life. Do not diagnose or guarantee safety on your own.

questions.prompt: Before handling food, someone proposes replacing handwashing with alcohol disinfection. What is appropriate?
choices: The smell of disinfectant means washing is unnecessary
Gloves make checking dirt unnecessary
Distinguish the purposes and procedures of washing and disinfection; disinfection alone does not replace washing
Skip both on busy days
questions.explanation: Do not collapse washing and hand disinfection into one task. Follow the facility’s hygiene procedure.

questions.prompt: When does the source say to confirm allergies and trigger foods?
choices: Ask the guest at booking or arrival and accurately share with the kitchen and responsible staff
Ask only after the meal
Infer the guest’s allergies from dish names
Wait until symptoms appear
questions.explanation: This asks when information is obtained, not only whether it is shared. Do not judge by dish names.

questions.prompt: Besides bread and noodles, what should be checked for wheat allergy?
choices: Only the color of the plate
Coatings, dumpling and other wrappers, breadcrumbs, and actual sauces, soy sauces and recipes
Only the dish’s price
No check is needed unless wheat appears in the dish name
questions.explanation: The source includes wrappers, coatings and condiments. Check actual products and recipes rather than making blanket claims.

illustration.caption: Keep the reported ingredient information connected through booking, preparation and service.
illustration.alt: The same guest identifier and ingredient marker matched on a reservation, kitchen check and serving slip
